reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: Almost all adult cases occur in current or former cigarette smokers, and the disease chiefly affects young to middle-aged adults
Presents with cough and breathlessness, though spontaneous pneumothorax is a common and sometimes recurrent mode of presentation
High-resolution CT shows a combination of nodules and cysts with an upper- and mid-zone predominance while relatively sparing the costophrenic angles
Cysts often evolve from earlier nodular and cavitary lesions as the disease progresses
Many cases harbour activating BRAF V600E or other MAPK-pathway mutations in the Langerhans cells, placing the disease within the spectrum of clonal histiocytic disorders
Smoking cessation is the cornerstone of management and can lead to stabilisation or regression of disease
Pulmonary hypertension can complicate advanced disease and is a major determinant of outcome
Diabetes insipidus or bone lesions may indicate multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis rather than isolated pulmonary involvement
reference.pathophysiology: PLCH is driven by accumulation and proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that form nodular lesions centred on small airways, provoking bronchiolar inflammation and later cystic destruction. Cigarette smoke is the principal trigger in adults, promoting recruitment and activation of these cells. Many lesions carry activating mutations in the MAPK signalling pathway (notably BRAF V600E), supporting a clonal, neoplastic component. Progressive airway-centred injury produces the characteristic mix of nodules and cysts, and vascular remodelling can lead to pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Other cystic lung diseases such as Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to characterise the nodule-and-cyst pattern and zonal distribution
Pulmonary function testing, which may show obstruction, restriction, or a mixed pattern with reduced diffusing capacity
Bronchoalveolar lavage and, where needed, lung biopsy with immunostaining (CD1a, langerin/CD207, S100)
Assessment for extrapulmonary disease including bone lesions and diabetes insipidus
Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension in advanced disease
redFlags: Acute pleuritic pain and breathlessness from spontaneous pneumothorax, which may recur
Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart strain in progressive disease
Progressive respiratory failure despite smoking cessation
Features of multisystem involvement such as new polyuria/polydipsia suggesting diabetes insipidus
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable; many patients stabilise or improve after stopping smoking, but a subset progress to extensive cystic disease, pulmonary hypertension, and respiratory failure that may require transplantation.
pitfalls: Not obtaining a detailed smoking history or failing to emphasise cessation as primary treatment
Confusing the cystic changes with emphysema or lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Overlooking pulmonary hypertension as a driver of symptoms and prognosis
Missing extrapulmonary manifestations that indicate systemic disease
